reasoning: The combination of sickle cell disease, abrupt tender splenomegaly, a substantial hemoglobin decline with preserved reticulocytosis, and shock without another bleeding source identifies acute splenic sequestration crisis. Ordered IV fluid resuscitation addresses hypovolemia, while expert-directed red-cell transfusion restores oxygen-carrying capacity without targeting a normal age-based hemoglobin. Serial splenic examination and combined laboratory-hemodynamic monitoring directly evaluate resolution and perfusion recovery.
selectionEvidence: Sudden tender splenic enlargement strongly localizes acute red-cell pooling to the spleen.
Hemoglobin fell sharply from 8.6 g/dL to 6.2 g/dL while the reticulocyte count remained elevated, arguing against marrow aplasia.
Heart rate 142/min, blood pressure 78/42 mm Hg, and capillary refill of 5 seconds demonstrate hemodynamic compromise requiring immediate volume support.
The absence of an external or internal bleeding source makes acute blood-loss anemia less likely.
Specialist-directed care with available IV fluid and red-cell transfusion orders supports controlled resuscitation and transfusion with serial assessment of the spleen, hemoglobin, and perfusion.
